blindSummary:
The country is in an active crackdown affecting trans visitors. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in the capital and in cities around the country on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per an international human-rights organisation. Public-indecency and sodomy provisions of the penal code (the latter carrying up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where a local trans advocacy NGO documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 a first-instance court in the capital refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as "mental illness." Since the president's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising has been crushed — one national LGBT organisation was dissolved.
blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.
blindSourceSummaries: International human-rights organisation (Feb 2025): this country steps up crackdown on LGBTI individuals with a wave of arrests - at least 84 people (mainly gay men and trans women) arrested, arbitrarily detained and unjustly prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 in the capital and cities across the country, solely based on actual or perceived SOGI, per a local civil-society association.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying international news outlet had covered the same wave of arrests in this country.

Rights-group country review: gender identities/expressions deviating from norms are effectively criminalised via the penal code's public-indecency and sodomy provisions, disproportionately targeting trans women; no comprehensive legal gender recognition framework - inconsistent rulings relying on judges' personal views and religious-law interpretations; gender-affirming care accessible only through well-informed medical professionals.

Local trans advocacy NGO (Nov 2024): transgender women in this country's prisons endure continuous suffering - processed under former names and gender identification in all official procedures; forced shaving on entry without consent causes profound psychological harm, targeting the essence of their gender identity.

Rights-group bulletin (Jan 2024): a first-instance court in the capital (April 2023) declined legal gender recognition to a trans man, asserting insufficient evidence of a biological medical condition and dismissing gender identity disorder as a mental illness not fulfilling legal-recognition criteria - reasoning based on comparative law from a neighbouring state, regional human-rights-court case-law and official religious opinions.

International human-rights organisation (March 2016): report on men prosecuted for homosexuality in this country - documents prosecutions under the sodomy provision and the use of forced anal examinations as 'evidence'.

Legal-rights database page for this country: a 2012 draft bill punishing 'insulting the sanctity of religion'; courts refused to ban an LGBT radio station (2018) and upheld an LGBT organisation's right to exist (2019) against government shutdown efforts.

International decriminalisation news platform (Sept 2017): this country pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing (a minister made the pledge at a UN session) but did not accept repeal of the sodomy provision (up to 3 years); the president of a national LGBT organisation was unenthusiastic - the abusive 'test' was dropped but the law remains.
blindTangential: The penal code's sodomy provision (up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
